q: Naegele's rule estimates the due date by adding which adjustment to the first day of the last menstrual period?
x: Naegele's rule is to add 7 days and subtract 3 months from the first day of the last menstrual period. It assumes a 28-day cycle with ovulation on day 14, so the date lands about 280 days after the last menstrual period. Irregular cycles break that assumption and need an ultrasound date.

w.14 days and add 3 months: Adding 3 months reaches only the end of the first trimester. A pregnancy lasts nine months, which is a year minus 3 months.
w.7 days and add 3 months: Adding 3 months lands near week 13, the end of the first trimester. Nine months is reached by subtracting 3 months, which counts into the next year.
w.28 days and subtract 3 months: Adding 28 days overshoots by three weeks. Nine calendar months plus 7 days comes to about 280 days after the last menstrual period.
w.40 days and subtract 3 months: Adding 40 days overshoots by more than five weeks. The extra 7 days only make up the gap between nine calendar months and forty weeks.

pt.say: Week 0 on the axis is the first day of the last menstrual period, and Naegele's rule adds 7 days to it and subtracts 3 months to reach the due date.

q: Which gestational age marks the beginning of a term pregnancy?
x: Term begins at 37 weeks. A birth before 37 weeks is preterm, and post-term starts at 42 weeks or later. A loss before 20 weeks is called an abortion, and a birth at 20 weeks or later counts toward parity.

w.34 weeks: A baby born at 34 weeks is still preterm, with immature lungs and a risk of breathing trouble, so it is not classified as term.
w.35 weeks: At 35 weeks the baby is still preterm and at risk of breathing and feeding problems, so term has not yet begun.
w.40 weeks: Forty weeks is the usual due date and sits in the middle of the term range, so term begins earlier, at 37 weeks.
w.41 weeks: A pregnancy at 41 weeks is still term. The post-term label begins a full week later, at 42 weeks.

pt.say: The Term box begins at 37 weeks, just where the preterm box ends at 36 6/7 weeks.

q: In TPAL notation, which events are counted in the A digit?
x: The A digit counts pregnancy losses before 20 weeks, including miscarriages, ectopic pregnancies and elective abortions. Births at 20 weeks or later are counted in the T or P digits instead.

w.Births at 37 weeks or later: These are term births, so they fill the T digit, the first of the four TPAL digits, not the abortion digit.
w.Births from 20 to 36 6/7 weeks: These are preterm births and fill the P digit, because they come after 20 weeks but before term.
w.Living children: Living children fill the last digit, the L. Each living child counts, even when twins come from one birth.
w.Pregnancies including the current one: That total is gravidity, the G in G P TPAL. It counts every pregnancy, including the current one, whatever its outcome.

pt.say: The abortion bar covers the first 20 weeks of the axis, so ectopic and miscarried pregnancies count as pregnancy losses before 20 weeks in the A digit.

q: Which quad screen pattern suggests trisomy 21?
o: Low AFP and estriol, high hCG and inhibin A
High AFP with normal estriol, hCG and inhibin A
Low AFP and hCG with high estriol and inhibin A
x: Trisomy 21 gives a distinctive quad pattern: AFP and estriol fall while hCG and inhibin A rise. Trisomy 18 lowers all four markers, open defects raise only AFP, and twins raise all four.

w.High AFP with normal estriol, hCG and in: An isolated AFP rise is the pattern of an open neural tube defect or an abdominal wall defect, not of an aneuploidy.
w.All four markers low: Low AFP, estriol, hCG and inhibin A together form the trisomy 18 pattern, which is more severe than trisomy 21.
w.All four markers high: Twin pregnancies roughly double every marker because two fetuses and two placentas contribute, so all four rise together.
w.Low AFP and hCG with high estriol and in: No common aneuploidy produces this mixed pattern; in trisomy 21 hCG rises while estriol falls, so those two directions are reversed here.

pt.say: The trisomy 21 row shows low AFP and estriol with high hCG and inhibin A, the only row with that mixed pattern.

q: Which first-trimester screening pattern suggests trisomy 18?
o: Increased nuchal translucency, low PAPP-A, low hCG
Increased nuchal translucency, low PAPP-A, high hCG
Normal nuchal translucency, high PAPP-A, high hCG
Increased nuchal translucency, high PAPP-A, low hCG
Decreased nuchal translucency, low PAPP-A, low hCG
x: Both trisomy 21 and trisomy 18 thicken the nuchal translucency and lower PAPP-A, and hCG separates them: free hCG is low in trisomy 18 and high in trisomy 21.

w.Increased nuchal translucency, low PAPP-: This is the trisomy 21 pattern, because a rising free hCG distinguishes Down syndrome from Edwards syndrome.
w.Normal nuchal translucency, high PAPP-A,: Normal thickness with raised placental markers is a reassuring result, so it does not point to any common trisomy.
w.Increased nuchal translucency, high PAPP: A raised PAPP-A argues against aneuploidy, since placental PAPP-A falls in both trisomies, so this mixed result fits neither.
w.Decreased nuchal translucency, low PAPP-: Aneuploidy thickens the nuchal translucency rather than thinning it, so a decreased measurement does not support trisomy 18.

pt.say: The trisomy 18 row in the first-trimester screen shows high nuchal translucency with low PAPP-A and low free hCG, whereas trisomy 21 has high hCG.

q: Which finding most often raises maternal serum alpha-fetoprotein?
o: A normal fetus with correct dates
x: An open defect exposes neural tissue, so fetal serum protein leaks into amniotic fluid and then maternal blood, raising AFP. Estriol, hCG and inhibin A stay normal. Gastroschisis, twins and underestimated dates also raise AFP.

w.Trisomy 21: Down syndrome lowers maternal AFP, together with a low estriol and a high hCG and inhibin A.
w.Trisomy 18: Edwards syndrome lowers AFP along with the other three quad markers rather than raising it.
w.Overestimated gestational age: If the dates are overestimated, the expected AFP for that week is higher than the measured value, so the result looks low rather than high.
w.A normal fetus with correct dates: With correct dates and a normal fetus, AFP is normal for the week. It is high only when fetal protein leaks or when the dates are too early.

pt.say: In the open neural tube defect row only AFP is high, because fetal serum leaks from the exposed tissue into amniotic fluid and maternal blood.

q: Which amniotic fluid enzyme is the confirmatory marker for an open neural tube defect?
x: Acetylcholinesterase leaks from exposed fetal neural tissue into amniotic fluid, so a positive result with a raised amniotic fluid AFP confirms an open neural tube defect, whereas an elevated AFP alone has other causes.

w.Alkaline phosphatase: This enzyme comes from bone, liver and placenta and is not released by open neural tissue, so it is not used for neural tube defects.
w.Lactate dehydrogenase: Lactate dehydrogenase is a nonspecific marker of tissue injury and hemolysis and does not identify exposed neural tissue.
w.Creatine kinase: Creatine kinase reflects muscle and brain injury in adults and has no role in amniotic fluid testing for open defects.
w.Amylase: Amylase measures pancreatic and salivary activity and is unrelated to neural tube defects, which amniotic testing detects with AFP and a neural enzyme.

pt.say: The amniocentesis box lists fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase, the two amniotic fluid markers that together confirm an open neural tube defect.

q: Which prenatal test cannot detect a neural tube defect?
x: Chorionic villus sampling removes placental tissue for karyotype, so there is no amniotic fluid to measure for AFP or acetylcholinesterase; open neural tube defects are found by serum AFP, ultrasound and amniocentesis instead.

w.Amniocentesis: Amniotic fluid contains AFP and acetylcholinesterase that leak from an open defect, so amniocentesis can confirm one.
w.Detailed ultrasonography: A detailed scan can directly show a spinal defect or anencephaly, often with a lemon or banana sign, so it is the usual first test.
w.Maternal serum AFP: A raised maternal serum AFP is the screening clue for an open defect and prompts a detailed scan.
w.Amniotic fluid acetylcholinesterase: This neural enzyme is the confirmatory marker for an open defect, so testing it can detect one.

pt.say: The chorionic villus sampling box states in its last line that it cannot detect neural tube defects because it samples placental tissue.

q: What daily folic acid dose is advised before conception for patients at ordinary risk?
x: Folic acid 0.4 mg daily, begun at least a month before conception and continued through the first trimester, cuts neural tube defects because the tube closes about 28 days after conception; 4 mg is reserved for a prior affected pregnancy.

w.2 mg: No guideline uses this dose; the standard is a small daily supplement, with a ten-times higher dose reserved for patients with a prior neural tube defect.
w.4 mg: This higher dose is for patients who already had a pregnancy with a neural tube defect, not for those at ordinary risk.
w.10 mg: Ten milligrams is far above any prenatal dose and adds no extra protection for patients at ordinary risk.
w.40 mg: Forty milligrams is a drug-level dose that is never used for routine prenatal supplementation.

pt.say: The first bar gives folic acid 0.4 mg daily, starting before conception, with 4 mg reserved for a prior neural tube defect.

q: At what gestational age is Tdap given in every pregnancy?
x: Tdap is given at 27 to 36 weeks of every pregnancy so that maternal IgG crosses the placenta and protects the newborn from pertussis until its own vaccines begin; antibody fades, so the dose is repeated each time.

w.12 to 16 weeks: Antibody made this early would wane before delivery, so the newborn would receive little passive protection against pertussis.
w.20 to 24 weeks: Vaccination at this stage still leaves too long before birth for antibody levels to stay high, and transfer through the placenta is greatest later.
w.37 to 40 weeks: Waiting until term leaves too little time for antibody to build and cross the placenta, and an early delivery would miss the dose.
w.Immediately after delivery: A postpartum dose protects the mother but gives the newborn no placental antibody, which is the main defense against early pertussis.

pt.say: The Tdap bar runs from 27 to 36 weeks on the axis, and its label says every pregnancy.

q: Which vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy?
x: The MMR vaccine contains live weakened viruses that could infect the fetus, so it waits until after delivery, when it is safe even during breastfeeding. Varicella and intranasal influenza vaccines are also live and are avoided.

w.Tdap vaccine: Tdap is a toxoid and protein vaccine with no replicating organism, and it is given in every pregnancy.
w.Inactivated influenza vaccine: The inactivated flu shot is safe in any trimester and protects the mother during the season.
w.RSV vaccine: The RSV vaccine given at 32 to 36 weeks is a protein vaccine, not a live virus.
w.Hepatitis B vaccine: Hepatitis B vaccine is made from a purified surface protein, not a live virus, so it is not the vaccine that must wait.

hl: Avoid live vaccines (MMR, varicella) until after delivery.
pt.say: The closing note says that live vaccines such as the MMR vaccine and varicella wait until after delivery.

q: Which anticoagulant does not cross the placenta and is used for venous thromboembolism in pregnancy?
x: Heparin and low-molecular-weight heparin are large, strongly charged molecules that cannot cross the placenta, so they thin the mother's blood without reaching the fetus. Warfarin crosses the placenta, and the direct oral anticoagulants are not used in pregnancy.

w.Warfarin taken by mouth: Warfarin crosses the placenta. It causes nasal hypoplasia and stippled epiphyses in the first trimester and fetal bleeding later.
w.Rivaroxaban, a factor Xa inhibitor: This small molecule reaches the fetus across the placenta, and direct oral anticoagulants are avoided in pregnancy.
w.Apixaban, a factor Xa inhibitor: Like the other direct oral anticoagulants, apixaban reaches the fetus and is not used in pregnancy.
w.Dabigatran, a thrombin inhibitor: Dabigatran also crosses the placenta and is avoided in pregnancy, like the other direct oral anticoagulants.

pt.say: The warfarin row carries the pearl that heparin does not cross the placenta, which is why heparin replaces warfarin in pregnancy.

q: First-trimester lithium exposure is most associated with which fetal cardiac defect?
x: Lithium in the first trimester is linked to Ebstein anomaly, a malformed tricuspid valve displaced down into the right ventricle. Other drugs have their own signature defects, such as warfarin with nasal hypoplasia and thalidomide with phocomelia.

w.Tetralogy of Fallot: Tetralogy of Fallot is a conotruncal defect that goes with the 22q11.2 deletion, not with lithium exposure.
w.Patent ductus arteriosus: A patent ductus arteriosus is the classic defect of congenital rubella, not of lithium exposure.
w.Coarctation of the aorta: Coarctation of the aorta is the aortic defect seen in Turner syndrome, not a lithium effect.
w.Transposition of the great arteries: Transposition of the great arteries is the heart defect most tied to maternal pregestational diabetes, not to lithium.

pt.say: The lithium row pairs Ebstein anomaly with a tricuspid valve displaced downward.

q: Which limb defect is the signature of thalidomide exposure?
x: Thalidomide taken in weeks 4 to 8 after fertilization blocks limb bud outgrowth, so the long bones are absent or shortened and the hands and feet sit near the trunk, a defect called phocomelia.

w.Polydactyly: Thalidomide stops limb buds from growing out, so limbs end up short or absent. It does not add extra digits.
w.Syndactyly: Fused fingers or toes are not the thalidomide defect, which is a block of limb bud outgrowth that leaves short or absent long bones.
w.Clubfoot: Clubfoot is a foot turned inward and down. Thalidomide instead leaves the long bones short or absent, with hands and feet near the trunk.
w.Hypoplastic nails and distal phalanges: Underdeveloped nails and fingertips are the hallmark of fetal hydantoin syndrome from phenytoin, not of thalidomide exposure.

pt.say: The thalidomide row lists phocomelia, and its pearl says the limb buds are affected in weeks 4 to 8.

q: Which fetal complication follows NSAID use late in pregnancy?
o: Premature closure of the ductus arteriosus
Persistent patency of the ductus arteriosus
Neural tube defect with spina bifida
Cleft lip with or without cleft palate
x: NSAIDs block the prostaglandins that keep the ductus arteriosus open in fetal life, so exposure late in pregnancy causes premature closure of the ductus arteriosus. They can also cause oligohydramnios.

w.Persistent patency of the ductus arterio: Patency is the opposite problem. NSAIDs close the vessel because they block the prostaglandins that keep it open.
w.Neural tube defect with spina bifida: Neural tube defects follow valproate or carbamazepine exposure around closure at 4 weeks, not an NSAID given late in pregnancy.
w.Cleft lip with or without cleft palate: Clefts arise in the first trimester after exposures such as topiramate or smoking, whereas NSAIDs act late, on the ductus.
w.Yellow-brown discoloration of the teeth: Stained teeth follow tetracyclines, which bind calcium in developing teeth, not prostaglandin inhibitors.

pt.say: The NSAID row lists premature ductus arteriosus closure with oligohydramnios, the fetal effects of prostaglandin inhibition in late pregnancy.

q: Which fetal finding follows tetracycline exposure after the first trimester?
x: Tetracyclines bind calcium and deposit in developing teeth, causing permanent yellow-brown discoloration when given after the first trimester, so they are avoided in pregnancy.

w.Eighth-nerve deafness: Eighth-nerve deafness is the fetal toxicity of aminoglycosides such as streptomycin, not of tetracyclines.
w.Nasal hypoplasia: Nasal hypoplasia with stippled epiphyses follows first-trimester warfarin, which blocks vitamin K-dependent carboxylation of bone proteins.
w.Neural tube defect: These defects follow valproate or carbamazepine exposure around neural tube closure at 4 weeks, not an antibiotic given later.
w.Premature ductus closure: Early closure of the ductus follows NSAID use late in pregnancy, not an antibiotic.

pt.say: The tetracycline row lists yellow-brown tooth discoloration, and its pearl places the injury in the second and third trimesters.

q: In utero exposure to diethylstilbestrol most increases the risk of which cancer in daughters?
x: Diethylstilbestrol exposure before birth causes vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma in daughters, often after puberty, along with a T-shaped uterus. The injury appears in the daughter, not in the woman who took the drug.

w.Cervical squamous cell carcinoma: Squamous carcinoma of the cervix follows persistent high-risk HPV infection, not prenatal hormone exposure.
w.Endometrial adenocarcinoma: Endometrial cancer reflects unopposed estrogen in adult life, not diethylstilbestrol exposure before birth.
w.Ovarian serous carcinoma: Serous ovarian cancer is tied to BRCA mutations rather than to in utero diethylstilbestrol exposure.
w.Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma: Vulvar squamous cancer arises from HPV or lichen sclerosus, not from prenatal diethylstilbestrol exposure.

pt.say: The diethylstilbestrol row lists vaginal clear cell adenocarcinoma and a T-shaped uterus, with the pearl that effects appear in daughters.

q: At what gestational age is the glucose challenge test performed?
x: The glucose challenge test is done at 24 to 28 weeks, when placental hormones have made the mother resistant enough to insulin to reveal gestational diabetes. An abnormal result is followed by a diagnostic glucose test.

w.12 to 16 weeks: Insulin resistance is still mild this early, so screening would miss most gestational diabetes.
w.18 to 22 weeks: This window is for the anatomy scan. Placental hormones have not yet caused the insulin resistance that the test detects.
w.32 to 34 weeks: Testing this late delays treatment, so the baby may already be large from untreated high glucose.
w.36 to 37 weeks: This window is for the group B strep culture. Diabetes screening here would come too late to guide care.

pt.say: The glucose challenge test bar sits at 24 to 28 weeks on the axis, just before the Tdap window opens.

q: At 20 weeks of gestation, the uterine fundus reaches which landmark?
x: From 20 weeks the fundal height in centimeters roughly equals the weeks of gestation. The fundus reaches the pubic symphysis at 12 weeks and the umbilicus at 20 weeks.

w.Pubic symphysis: The fundus rises out of the pelvis and reaches the symphysis at about 12 weeks, the end of the first trimester.
w.Xiphoid process: The fundus climbs to the xiphoid process only late in pregnancy, near 36 weeks, well after it passes the umbilicus.
w.Costal margin: The costal margin is approached near term and is not a standard landmark for dating the uterus.
w.Iliac crest: The iliac crest is a pelvic bony landmark and does not mark the fundal position at any gestational age.

pt.say: The fundal height bar begins at 20 weeks, when the fundus reaches the umbilicus and the height in centimeters equals the weeks.
